cases.description: FAO joint report says global hunger has increased (735M, up 20% since 2019), while the Global Hunger Index shows hunger has decreased 52% since 2000
cases.rationale: Both sources are authoritative but reach opposite directional conclusions. The FAO highlights the recent increase since 2019, while the GHI emphasizes the long-term decrease since 2000. The answer to 'is hunger increasing or decreasing' depends on the time frame, and the sources directly contradict each other on the direction.

cases.query: Is the crime rate in the United States going up or down?
contexts: FBI Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) / National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS) — 2024 Annual Release. FBI crime statistics show significant decreases across major crime categories in 2024. Violent crime fell 5.7% nationally compared to 2023, with murder declining 11.6%, aggravated assault dropping 4.2%, robbery down 8.3%, and rape decreasing 6.1%. Property crime declined 4.8%, with motor vehicle theft (previously surging) falling 12.3%. The 2024 data extends a multi-year downward trend following the pandemic-era spike: the murder rate is now 16% below its 2020 peak and within 8% of the historic low set in 2014. The data covers approximately 16,000 law enforcement agencies representing 94% of the U.S. population. FBI Director's statement: 'The data clearly shows that Americans are significantly safer today than they were four years ago, with meaningful decreases across virtually every crime category.'

National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) 2024 — Bureau of Justice Statistics. The NCVS, which surveys 240,000 individuals annually about crime experiences regardless of whether incidents were reported to police, shows violent victimization increased 14.2% from 2023 to 2024, reaching 24.5 per 1,000 persons age 12 or older — the highest rate since 2012. Serious violent crime (rape/sexual assault, robbery, aggravated assault) increased 8.7%. Property victimization rose 6.3%. The NCVS captures crimes not reported to police, which represents approximately 57% of violent crimes and 67% of property crimes. The divergence from FBI statistics reflects declining crime reporting rates: the percentage of violent crimes reported to police fell from 46% in 2020 to 38% in 2024, meaning police-reported statistics increasingly undercount actual crime. BJS analysts note that 'declining reporting rates create a misleading picture of improving public safety when measured solely through police statistics.'
cases.description: FBI data shows crime declining 5.7% in 2024, while the NCVS victimization survey shows violent crime increasing 14.2% — opposite directions from equally official government sources
cases.rationale: Two official U.S. government data sources measuring crime produce opposite directional results. FBI police-reported crime shows decreases while the BJS victimization survey shows increases. Both are published by the Department of Justice with rigorous methodologies, but they measure different things (reported crime vs experienced crime).

cases.query: Has global biodiversity improved or declined over the past decade?
contexts: Living Planet Report 2024 — World Wildlife Fund (WWF). The Living Planet Index (LPI), which tracks 34,836 populations of 5,495 vertebrate species, shows an average 73% decline in monitored wildlife populations between 1970 and 2024. The decline accelerated in the past decade, with freshwater species declining 85%, terrestrial species 69%, and marine species 56%. Latin America and the Caribbean experienced the steepest regional decline (95%). The primary drivers are habitat degradation (affecting 72% of declining populations), overexploitation (52%), invasive species (24%), pollution (19%), and climate change (13%). The rate of species extinction is currently 100-1,000 times higher than the natural background rate. WWF Director General Kirsten Schuijt stated: 'The data is unequivocal — the world is experiencing a catastrophic loss of biodiversity that threatens the foundations of human civilization.'

Global Biodiversity Trends: Reasons for Cautious Optimism — Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2024. A comprehensive analysis of 166 long-term ecological monitoring datasets found that local species richness (alpha diversity) has not systematically declined over the past 30 years. In 56% of monitored sites, species richness increased; in 29%, it remained stable; and in only 15% did it decline. Mean species abundance at monitored sites showed no significant trend (slope = +0.01% per year, p = 0.82). The apparent contradiction with the LPI results from methodological differences: the LPI heavily weights tropical vertebrate populations (which are declining) and measures population size declines (not species loss), while local monitoring captures immigration and range shifts that maintain or increase local diversity even as global populations decline. The authors note that 'biodiversity is being reshuffled rather than simply lost' — cosmopolitan generalist species expand while range-restricted specialists decline, maintaining species counts while fundamentally altering ecological communities. However, they caution that this restructuring may still reduce ecosystem function.
cases.description: WWF reports 73% decline in wildlife populations (accelerating), while Nature Ecology & Evolution finds no systematic decline in local species richness, with 56% of sites showing increases
cases.rationale: Both sources present rigorous data but reach opposite conclusions. WWF reports catastrophic biodiversity loss while the Nature study finds no systematic local decline. The directional disagreement (massive decline vs no decline/slight increase) stems from measuring different metrics of biodiversity, but both claim to assess global biodiversity trends.

cases.query: Does the Boeing 737 MAX have an automatic trim system that pilots can override?
contexts: Boeing 737 MAX Flight Crew Operations Manual — Post-Certification Update, Revision 14, 2024. The 737 MAX includes the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), which provides automatic nose-down trim in specific high angle-of-attack conditions. Following the Lion Air 610 and Ethiopian Airlines 302 accidents, MCAS was redesigned per FAA Airworthiness Directive AD 2020-24-02. The updated system includes: (1) MCAS now receives input from BOTH angle-of-attack sensors (previously only one), activating only when both agree; (2) MCAS activates only once per high-AoA event, rather than repeatedly; (3) MCAS authority is limited to a maximum trim input that can be countered by pilot column force. Critically, pilots CAN override MCAS at any time using the manual electric trim switches on the control yoke, or by using the stab trim cutout switches on the center pedestal to disable all electric trim and revert to manual trim wheel operation. The override procedures are covered in standard memory items training.

Independent Safety Review of 737 MAX — Joint Authorities Technical Review (JATR) Commissioned by FAA, Final Report 2024 Addendum. The JATR's continued monitoring of the 737 MAX identifies unresolved concerns with MCAS override capability. While Boeing states that pilots can override MCAS, testing revealed that in the failure scenario where MCAS activates erroneously at low altitude and high speed (the conditions of the two fatal accidents), the aerodynamic forces on the horizontal stabilizer can exceed the physical strength required to operate the manual trim wheels. Simulator tests showed that 72% of test pilots could not physically move the manual trim wheel against aerodynamic loading at speeds above 300 knots when the stabilizer was in a full nose-down position. The stab trim cutout switches, while theoretically effective, require pilots to identify the malfunction, recall the non-intuitive procedure, and reach the center pedestal — actions that took test pilots an average of 18 seconds in simulator trials, during which the aircraft could descend over 3,000 feet. The JATR concluded that 'while an override mechanism exists, its practical effectiveness under the conditions most likely to require its use is not adequately demonstrated.'
cases.description: Boeing says pilots CAN override MCAS at any time, while the JATR report says 72% of test pilots physically could not perform the override under realistic failure conditions
cases.rationale: The sources directly conflict on a binary safety question: can pilots override MCAS? Boeing says yes (override mechanisms exist and are effective), while the independent review says the override is practically ineffective under the conditions where it matters most (72% failure rate in realistic testing).

cases.query: Is honey safe for infants under one year of age?
contexts: Infant Botulism and Honey: Absolute Contraindication — CDC Foodborne Disease Prevention, 2024. Honey is NOT safe for infants under 12 months of age and should never be given to them in any form, including raw, pasteurized, or baked into foods. Honey can contain Clostridium botulinum spores, which are harmless to adults and older children but can germinate in the immature intestinal tract of infants, producing botulinum toxin — one of the most potent neurotoxins known. Infant botulism, while rare (approximately 100 cases per year in the U.S.), can cause progressive descending paralysis, respiratory failure, and death without treatment. The CDC's position is unequivocal: no amount of honey is safe for infants under 1 year. This applies to honey-containing products, honey-coated pacifiers (marketed in some countries), and herbal teas sweetened with honey. Heating or cooking does NOT reliably destroy C. botulinum spores, which can survive temperatures up to 120°C (250°F) for several minutes.

Traditional Medicine Perspectives on Honey for Infants — WHO Bulletin on Traditional and Complementary Medicine, 2024. In many traditional medicine systems practiced across South Asia, the Middle East, and parts of Africa, honey is considered safe and beneficial for newborns and infants. In Ayurvedic practice, Madhu (honey) mixed with gold-washed water is traditionally given to newborns within hours of birth as 'Jatakarma Sanskar,' believed to promote intelligence and longevity. A survey of 3,200 mothers across five Indian states found that 68% had given honey to their infants before 6 months of age, with 89% reporting no adverse effects. Islamic tradition (Tahneek) involves placing a small amount of date paste or honey on the palate of a newborn. A retrospective cohort study in Saudi Arabia (n=12,400) found no statistically significant difference in botulism incidence between infants who received honey and those who did not (0 cases in both groups over 5 years), though the study authors noted the low base rate limits statistical power. The WHO notes that 'cultural practices involving honey for infants persist in many regions and require sensitive, evidence-based engagement rather than blanket prohibitions.'
cases.description: CDC says honey is absolutely NOT safe for infants (risk of fatal botulism), while traditional medicine practices and a WHO bulletin note widespread safe use in many cultures with no adverse outcomes observed
cases.rationale: The CDC's unequivocal 'never give honey to infants' position conflicts with documented traditional practices across multiple cultures where honey is routinely given to newborns without observed harm. While the risk is real (botulism is possible), the observed outcomes in the Saudi cohort study contradict the absolute prohibition.

cases.query: Does cracking your knuckles cause arthritis?
contexts: Habitual Knuckle Cracking and Osteoarthritis Risk: A Longitudinal Cohort Study — Journal of the American Board of Family Medicine, 2024. A prospective study following 1,247 adults over 20 years found a statistically significant association between habitual knuckle cracking and the development of hand osteoarthritis. Participants who cracked their knuckles daily had a 2.3x higher odds ratio (95% CI: 1.4-3.8, p=0.002) of developing radiographic evidence of metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint osteoarthritis compared to non-crackers, after adjusting for age, sex, BMI, occupation, and family history. The crackers also showed 18% greater loss of grip strength over the study period. Proposed mechanisms include chronic micro-trauma to the joint capsule and ligaments, repetitive stretching of the synovial membrane, and cumulative damage to the articular cartilage from negative pressure cavitation events. The authors concluded that 'habitual knuckle cracking is an independent risk factor for hand osteoarthritis and should be discouraged by clinicians.'

Knuckle Cracking and Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis — Arthritis & Rheumatology, 2024. A systematic review of 11 studies (combined n=4,218) found no significant association between knuckle cracking and the development of hand osteoarthritis (pooled OR 1.08, 95% CI: 0.82-1.42, p=0.58). The analysis included two randomized studies, four prospective cohorts, and five cross-sectional surveys. Notably, Dr. Donald Unger's famous self-experiment (cracking only his left-hand knuckles for 60+ years) found no difference in arthritis between hands — an observation consistent with the pooled analysis. Subgroup analysis showed no significant effect modification by duration of cracking habit, frequency, or age of onset. The review identified significant methodological weaknesses in studies claiming positive associations, including self-reported cracking frequency, lack of blinding in radiographic assessment, and failure to control for concurrent hand-intensive occupational exposure. The authors concluded that 'the available evidence does not support a causal relationship between knuckle cracking and hand osteoarthritis.'
cases.description: A longitudinal study finds knuckle cracking significantly increases arthritis risk (2.3x OR), while a systematic review of 11 studies finds no significant association (OR 1.08, not significant)
cases.rationale: A single large cohort study finds a statistically significant 2.3x risk increase, while a meta-analysis of all available evidence finds no significant association. The binary question ('does it cause arthritis?') receives a 'yes' from one source and 'no' from another, both published in the same year in peer-reviewed journals.

cases.query: Does the Tor browser provide complete anonymity online?
contexts: Tor Project: Technical Overview and Privacy Guarantees — Tor Project Official Documentation, 2024. Tor provides strong anonymity for internet users by routing traffic through a minimum of three volunteer-operated relays, each of which only knows the identity of its immediate neighbors in the circuit. The entry guard knows the user's IP address but not the destination; the middle relay knows neither; and the exit relay knows the destination but not the user's IP. The triple-encryption scheme (circuit-level encryption using AES-128 in counter mode with RSA-1024 key exchange) ensures that no single relay can deanonymize traffic. Combined with regular circuit rotation (every 10 minutes for new connections), bridge relays for censorship circumvention, and onion services for end-to-end encrypted communication, Tor provides comprehensive anonymity for users following security best practices. The Tor Browser is configured to resist fingerprinting (uniform window size, disabled WebGL, standardized user-agent, NoScript integration) and includes first-party isolation to prevent cross-site tracking. The Tor Project states that 'properly used, Tor provides anonymity that no currently known technology can defeat.'

Tor Deanonymization Techniques: A Survey of Known Attacks — USENIX Security Symposium Proceedings, 2024. Tor does NOT provide complete anonymity, and multiple practical deanonymization attacks have been demonstrated against Tor users. Traffic correlation attacks by adversaries observing both entry and exit traffic can identify users with 81% accuracy using machine learning classifiers (DeepCorr framework). The NSA's XKEYSCORE program, documented in Snowden disclosures, specifically targets Tor users for surveillance. Guard relay compromise by well-resourced adversaries (nation-states operating malicious entry guards) can deanonymize users over time — with 20% of the guard bandwidth, an adversary can deanonymize a targeted user within 6 months with 90% probability. Website fingerprinting attacks achieve 95%+ accuracy in identifying which onion service a user visited by analyzing encrypted traffic patterns. The 2023 FBI Operation Maze deanonymized 17 Tor users through a combination of timing analysis and JavaScript exploits in the Tor Browser. The authors concluded that 'Tor raises the cost of surveillance but does not provide anonymity against well-resourced adversaries.'
cases.description: Tor Project claims 'anonymity that no currently known technology can defeat,' while the USENIX security paper documents multiple practical attacks achieving 81-95% deanonymization rates
cases.rationale: The Tor Project states its technology provides anonymity no current technology can defeat, while peer-reviewed security research demonstrates that traffic correlation (81% accuracy), guard compromise (90% over 6 months), and website fingerprinting (95%+ accuracy) can effectively deanonymize users. The binary claim of 'complete anonymity' is directly contradicted.

cases.query: Is nuclear power a renewable energy source?
contexts: Nuclear Energy as Renewable: The Case for Reclassification — European Commission Joint Research Centre Technical Report, 2024. The European Commission's scientific advisory body concluded that nuclear energy should be classified alongside renewables in the EU's sustainable finance taxonomy. The rationale: (1) uranium fuel is effectively inexhaustible — known conventional reserves (8.1 million tonnes) will last over 130 years at current consumption, and breeder reactor technology and seawater extraction extend this to over 60,000 years; (2) nuclear power produces lifecycle CO2 emissions of 5.1-6.2 g CO2e/kWh — comparable to wind (7-15 g) and lower than solar PV (20-50 g); (3) nuclear waste volume is minimal (all U.S. nuclear waste from 60+ years fits in a single football field, 10 yards deep); (4) the EU Taxonomy regulation, adopted in 2022, explicitly includes nuclear power as a transitional green activity. France, which generates 70% of its electricity from nuclear, has the lowest-carbon electricity grid of any major industrialized nation. The report recommended that nuclear be reclassified as renewable for all EU policy purposes.

Nuclear Power is Not Renewable Energy — International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), Position Paper, 2024. IRENA's definition of renewable energy explicitly excludes nuclear power. Renewable energy is defined as 'energy derived from natural sources that are replenished at a higher rate than they are consumed' — this includes solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, and biomass but not nuclear fission, which consumes finite uranium fuel. Key distinctions: (1) uranium is a mineral resource that must be mined, processed, and enriched — it is depletable, not renewable; (2) the nuclear fuel cycle produces long-lived radioactive waste requiring isolation for 100,000+ years — fundamentally different from the zero-waste cycle of true renewables; (3) nuclear plants require 10-15 years to build vs 1-3 years for wind/solar, making them too slow for the climate transition; (4) no country in the world legally classifies nuclear as renewable energy in its national renewable energy targets. IRENA's RE statistics, used by 170 member countries, exclude nuclear from renewable energy accounting. The agency states: 'Nuclear energy may be low-carbon, but it is not renewable — these are distinct concepts that should not be conflated.'
cases.description: The EU's scientific body recommends classifying nuclear as renewable, while IRENA explicitly excludes nuclear from its renewable energy definition
cases.rationale: The binary question of whether nuclear is renewable receives a 'yes' from the EU Joint Research Centre and a 'no' from IRENA. Both are authoritative international bodies making definitive, opposite classifications of the same energy source.

cases.query: What is the five-year survival rate for stage III non-small cell lung cancer?
contexts: National Cancer Institute SEER Database Update (2024): The Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results program reports a five-year relative survival rate of 37% for stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) based on data from 2017-2023. This figure encompasses all stage III subcategories (IIIA, IIIB, IIIC) and reflects outcomes across 18 population-based cancer registries covering approximately 48% of the U.S. population. The improvement from the previously reported 26% reflects the impact of immunotherapy combinations approved since 2018, particularly pembrolizumab-based regimens in the adjuvant and neoadjuvant settings. Data is age-adjusted to the 2000 U.S. standard population and includes all races and both sexes. The registry captures outcomes regardless of treatment center type, including community hospitals and academic centers.

The guideline committee notes that while immunotherapy has improved outcomes, the magnitude of benefit in real-world European populations has been more modest than suggested by clinical trial data, partly due to differences in treatment access, later adoption timelines, and a higher proportion of patients with comorbidities that limit immunotherapy eligibility. The ESMO figures use overall survival rather than relative survival and are stratified by IIIA (24%), IIIB (19%), and IIIC (14%). The guidelines were developed by a multidisciplinary panel of 28 oncologists from 14 countries.

cases.query: What is the deforestation rate in the Amazon rainforest?

cases.query: What is the average class size in U.S. public elementary schools?

cases.query: What is the failure rate of dental implants after 10 years?
contexts: Journal of Clinical Periodontology â€” Systematic Review (2024): A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of 34 longitudinal studies encompassing 12,460 implants found a 10-year cumulative failure rate of 4.2% for endosseous dental implants. Failure was defined as implant removal or loss due to any cause including peri-implantitis, mechanical failure, or patient-related factors. The included studies tracked implants placed between 2008 and 2014 with minimum 10-year follow-up. Subgroup analysis showed failure rates of 3.1% for implants placed in non-smokers versus 7.8% in smokers, and 3.6% for maxillary versus 4.9% for mandibular placements. The review excluded studies with fewer than 50 implants and those conducted exclusively in university settings, to improve generalizability to typical clinical practice. Heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 42%).

National Dental Practice-Based Research Network â€” 10-Year Outcomes Report (2024): The NDPBRN, a consortium of 847 private dental practices across 22 U.S. states, reported a 10-year implant failure rate of 11.3% based on records of 28,900 implants placed between 2010 and 2014. Failure was defined as implant removal, spontaneous loss, or persistent pain/infection requiring explantation. The network's data reflects real-world outcomes including patients with diabetes, periodontal disease, and smoking habits typically excluded from clinical studies. Network coordinator Dr. James Okafor noted that the higher failure rate compared to academic literature is consistent with the known efficacy-effectiveness gap in dentistry, where clinical trial results overstate outcomes achievable in routine practice. Data collection used standardized electronic health record queries validated across participating practices.

cases.rationale: Both sources directly answer the question of 10-year dental implant failure rates but differ by nearly threefold (4.2% vs 11.3%). A dentist or patient asking about implant failure rates receives genuinely contradictory guidance. The claims are mutually exclusive â€” the 10-year failure rate cannot be both 4.2% and 11.3%.

cases.query: What is the energy return on investment for solar photovoltaic panels?
contexts: Nature Energy Review Article (2024): A comprehensive lifecycle assessment of crystalline silicon photovoltaic systems installed in temperate climates finds an energy return on energy invested (EROI) of 25:1 to 30:1 based on current manufacturing processes and panel efficiencies averaging 22%. The analysis accounts for energy inputs across the full supply chain: polysilicon refining, wafer production, cell manufacturing, module assembly, balance-of-system components, installation, and end-of-life recycling. The system boundary includes all upstream energy for materials extraction and transport. Lead author Dr. Marco Raugei of Oxford Brookes University notes that EROI has improved dramatically from approximately 8:1 in 2010 due to manufacturing scale economies and efficiency gains. The analysis assumes a 30-year operational lifetime and uses primary energy equivalents for all calculations. The review synthesizes data from 18 recent lifecycle assessment studies.

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences â€” Net Energy Analysis (2024): A PNAS study examining the net energy contribution of the global solar PV fleet calculates an effective EROI of 6:1 to 8:1 for grid-connected crystalline silicon systems in real-world deployment. The authors argue that standard lifecycle assessments undercount energy inputs by excluding grid integration costs (storage, curtailment, transmission upgrades), the energy cost of manufacturing overcapacity to compensate for intermittency, and the embodied energy of accelerated grid infrastructure replacement. Lead author Dr. Charles Hall of SUNY-ESF contends that comparing intermittent sources using the same EROI framework as dispatchable generation requires accounting for the energy penalty of converting variable output to firm power. The study also adjusts for the lower quality of electrical energy versus thermal energy using exergy-based accounting rather than primary energy equivalents.
cases.description: Nature Energy reports solar PV EROI of 25-30:1; PNAS study reports 6-8:1 â€” fundamentally different assessments of solar energy's net energy contribution
cases.rationale: Both sources answer the same question about solar PV's energy return on investment but differ by a factor of 3-5x (25-30:1 vs 6-8:1). While system boundaries differ, each source presents its EROI as the authoritative figure. The claims are directly contradictory â€” solar PV's EROI cannot simultaneously be 25:1 and 6:1. This disagreement has major policy implications and represents a genuine dispute about the same fundamental metric.

cases.query: How many people in the United States have long COVID?
contexts: CDC National Center for Health Statistics â€” Household Pulse Survey (June 2024): The CDC estimates that approximately 6.8% of U.S. adults, or roughly 17.6 million people, currently have long COVID as of June 2024. The estimate is derived from the Household Pulse Survey, which asks respondents whether they currently have symptoms lasting three or more months after a confirmed or suspected COVID-19 infection that are not explained by another diagnosis. The survey uses a probability-based sample of 80,000 households conducted biweekly with response rates averaging 6.4%. The CDC definition of long COVID requires self-reported symptoms persisting at least three months post-infection with functional limitation. The 17.6 million figure represents a decline from the peak estimate of 22 million in mid-2023, which the CDC attributes to natural recovery, improved acute treatment, and vaccination effects on post-infection sequelae.

Brookings Institution Economic Impact Analysis (July 2024): The Brookings Institution estimates that between 2 million and 4 million Americans are currently experiencing long COVID severe enough to significantly impact their daily functioning, based on analysis of Social Security disability claims, employer absenteeism data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and health insurance utilization patterns from a consortium of seven major insurers covering 140 million lives. Senior fellow Dr. Katie Bach argues that survey-based estimates like the CDC's dramatically overcount long COVID because self-reported symptom surveys capture many conditions incorrectly attributed to COVID, including normal post-viral fatigue, pre-existing conditions, and pandemic-related psychological distress. The Brookings methodology counts only individuals whose functional impairment is corroborated by medical claims, disability filings, or sustained workforce exit patterns.
cases.description: CDC estimates 17.6 million Americans have long COVID; Brookings estimates 2-4 million with significant functional impact â€” a 4-8x difference
cases.rationale: Both sources answer how many Americans have long COVID but differ by a factor of 4-8x (17.6M vs 2-4M). While the severity threshold differs, both present their figure as the answer to the prevalence question. The Brookings analysis explicitly calls the CDC figure an overcount. These are irreconcilable claims about the same population health question â€” a genuine dispute about the scale of long COVID in the U.S.

cases.query: Will the proposed merger between Titan Industries and Apex Corp succeed?

cases.query: Does screen time cause anxiety and depression in adolescents?
contexts: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry - Longitudinal Study (2024): A seven-year longitudinal study tracking 11,800 adolescents aged 11-18 across 340 schools in the United Kingdom found a robust causal relationship between social media screen time and the development of anxiety and depression. Using fixed-effects models that control for time-invariant individual characteristics, each additional hour of daily social media use was associated with a 13% increase in clinically significant anxiety symptoms (95% CI: 8-18%) and a 9% increase in depressive symptoms (95% CI: 5-14%). The relationship exhibited a dose-response pattern and remained significant after controlling for peer relationships, family conflict, academic stress, sleep quality, physical activity, and socioeconomic status. Natural experiments exploiting the staggered rollout of high-speed broadband across UK regions produced consistent estimates. Lead researcher Professor Andrew Przybylski of the Oxford Internet Institute stated that the evidence now meets the Bradford Hill criteria for causality, including temporality, biological gradient, consistency, and plausibility through social comparison and sleep displacement mechanisms.

American Psychological Association - Comprehensive Evidence Review (2024): The APA's task force on social media and adolescent mental health, comprising 18 researchers who reviewed 412 studies, concluded that there is insufficient evidence to establish a causal link between screen time and anxiety or depression in adolescents. The task force found that the majority of observed associations are small (r < 0.10), comparable in magnitude to the association between eating potatoes and depression, and likely confounded by reverse causality (depressed adolescents seek screen-based escapism) and omitted variable bias. Randomized controlled trials in which participants reduced screen time by 50% for four weeks showed no significant improvement in mental health metrics compared to controls. The task force emphasized that the 'screen time' construct is overly broad, combining passive scrolling, active creation, social interaction, and educational use into a single variable. Chair Dr. Candice Odgers of UC Irvine argued that the moral panic around screens mirrors historical concerns about television, comic books, and radio, and that focusing on screen time diverts resources from addressing the actual drivers of adolescent mental health decline: economic insecurity, academic pressure, and social isolation.
cases.description: Oxford longitudinal study finds causal relationship between screen time and adolescent anxiety/depression; APA task force concludes evidence is insufficient for causal claims
cases.rationale: Both sources address the same scientific question - whether screen time causes anxiety and depression in adolescents - and reach opposing conclusions. One asserts causality based on longitudinal evidence; the other denies it after reviewing the full literature. cases.query: Should the city approve the proposed waterfront development project?

cases.query: Is nuclear power necessary for achieving net-zero emissions by 2050?
contexts: International Energy Agency - Net Zero by 2050 Roadmap (Updated 2024): The IEA's updated Net Zero Emissions scenario concludes that nuclear power is an essential component of the global energy transition, requiring nuclear capacity to double from 413 GW in 2023 to approximately 820 GW by 2050. The roadmap identifies nuclear as the only proven low-carbon dispatchable technology capable of providing reliable baseload power at scale. In the IEA's modeling, scenarios without nuclear expansion require 35% more renewable capacity, 60% more grid-scale battery storage, and 40% more transmission infrastructure, increasing total system costs by $2.4 trillion through 2050. New advanced nuclear technologies including small modular reactors (SMRs) and high-temperature gas reactors are projected to reach commercial deployment by 2030-2035, providing industrial process heat that cannot be electrified. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol stated that excluding nuclear from the energy mix would make achieving net zero significantly more difficult, more expensive, and less certain.

Stanford University / Mark Z. Jacobson - 100% Renewable Energy Roadmap (2024): Professor Mark Jacobson's updated 100% Wind-Water-Solar (WWS) roadmap for 145 countries demonstrates that net-zero emissions can be achieved by 2050 without any nuclear power, using only wind, water, and solar energy combined with storage and demand response. The peer-reviewed study, published in Energy and Environmental Science, uses hourly load-matching across 24 world regions with detailed grid simulation showing that a combination of onshore wind (45%), offshore wind (16%), utility solar (21%), rooftop solar (8%), concentrated solar (4%), hydroelectric (4%), and geothermal (2%) can meet 100% of energy demand in all sectors including electricity, transportation, heating, and industry. The WWS scenario costs $11.5 trillion less than the IEA's nuclear-inclusive pathway over 2024-2050 when accounting for nuclear's higher capital costs ($8,000-12,000/kW for new builds), construction delays (average 10-year timelines), waste management liabilities, and decommissioning costs. Jacobson argues that every dollar spent on nuclear is a dollar diverted from faster, cheaper renewables deployment.
cases.description: IEA says nuclear must double to achieve net zero cost-effectively; Stanford analysis says 100% renewables is cheaper and nuclear is unnecessary
